ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Within-subjects impossible for learning manipulation; df in ANOVA tables inconsistent
ground_truth.original_snippet: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single between-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables;
ground_truth.modified_snippet: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables;
ground_truth.description: Changed between-subjects to within-subjects — impossible for this intervention (learning about IVE permanently changes cognition); df in ANOVA tables are inconsistent with within-subjects

matched_finding.description: The original Small et al. (2007) studies used a between-subjects design where participants were randomly assigned to conditions. The replication states it 'embedded Studies 1 and 3 into a single within-subject design.' This is a fundamental design change that introduces demand characteristics, contrast effects, and order effects. Participants who see both identifiable and statistical victim conditions will likely recognize the manipulation and adjust their responses accordingly, which directly undermines the ecological validity of the identifiable victim effect manipulation. This change is not adequately justified and could explain null results.
matched_finding.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

ground_truth.modified_snippet: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

matched_finding.subcategory: self-selection into conditions rather than random assignment
matched_finding.description: The procedures section states that 'Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.' This means participants were not randomly assigned to conditions but instead self-selected. This completely invalidates any causal inference about the effect of identifiability or intervention on donation behavior, as self-selection introduces massive confounding. Participants who choose to learn about the identifiable victim effect may differ systematically from those who do not. This is a fatal flaw for a study attempting to replicate experimentally manipulated effects.
matched_finding.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

ground_truth.modified_snippet: meaning that participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).
ground_truth.description: Reversed which condition has higher donations — IVE is now reversed (statistical > identifiable), contradicting the phenomenon being replicated and Table 11 descriptives

matched_finding.subcategory: contradictory direction of identifiable victim effect in results
matched_finding.description: The identifiable victim effect predicts that people donate MORE to identifiable victims than statistical victims. However, the results report the opposite direction: 'participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).' This reversal is not discussed or explained. Furthermore, the descriptive statistics in Table 7 show the identifiable victim condition (M=2.58 intervention, M=2.50 no intervention) versus statistical victim condition (M=2.46 intervention, M=2.01 no intervention), which actually shows identifiable victims receiving more in the no-intervention condition—contradicting the text's claim about the direction of the effect.
matched_finding.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67)

The "availability heuristic"  (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated whe...
ground_truth.description: Replaced affect heuristic (emotional arousal) with availability heuristic (memory retrieval) — changes the theoretical mechanism; intervention design and feeling measures no longer match the theory

matched_finding.subcategory: availability heuristic misapplied to identifiable victim effect
matched_finding.description: The introduction attributes the identifiable victim effect to the 'availability heuristic,' which refers to judging frequency or probability based on ease of retrieval from memory. However, the identifiable victim effect is more accurately explained by the affect heuristic and identifiability per se—the emotional response to a specific, named individual. The availability heuristic is about memory retrieval ease, not emotional salience of identified individuals. This is a theoretical misattribution that conflates distinct psychological mechanisms. The affect heuristic (Slovic et al., 2007, which is even cited in the references) would be the more appropriate framework.
matched_finding.quote: The 'availability heuristic' (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual
